cues.text: Speaker 1: They lived in Holland.
We're color-blind.
We don't know what is yellow, or what is black, or what is white.
They always educated that all people are equal.
We so we could never imagine that anything like the Holocaust would happen in Holland.
My name is Avraham Ruth.
I was born in Holland in 1928.
I must say that we had a very good life till the war began, till 1940.
The first thing you feel, you are being put into a situation where you felt that you you are hunted. You are an hunted man.
The Germans started to persecute first of all the Jews.
First, we couldn't go to school, then we couldn't go to shops, we couldn't go with the with the tramway, we couldn't go on bicycles.
And you see here is written Central Station and so, we couldn't travel with the tram.
No, we had no transport.
We had to go everything walking.
Speaker 2: Like walking.
Speaker 1: Yes.
Here you see a typical thing, they made these sandbags.
Because at that time people thought that the sandbags would save them from the Germans.
On the 15th of May in 1940, when the when the Germans declared their victory,
I had a classmate of mine, a very good friend of mine, and his parents, so this family, the father, mother, and three children, they took their own life.
I was only at that time 12 years old.
We knew that it's not going right, it's going wrong.
The Jewish community started school for Jewish children.
I, myself, studied in a parallel class with Anne Frank.
But in this school it was very strange because you would go to school, you would never know what teacher would be the next day or what child would disappear.
And you didn't know if they went into hiding, if they went were sent to concentration camp.
And and when I see a class picture today, I I see about more than half of them, which I know have never returned.
Teachers who never came back.
Nothing.

There was a big house of orphans, the Dutch police came in there, and they didn't let anybody come near, they brought in trucks, and 170 children were sent all in the trucks to straight to Auschwitz, and also none of them came back.

The strange thing is that we never never believed that we would be exterminated. Maybe we were naive, or my parents were naive, the Jewish people were naive, they never understood what was going to happen to them.
My father had connections with the Dutch underground, and then the Dutch underground brought us to various addresses, each of my brothers on a separate address, where we were hidden during the war.
I, for myself, went up to a farmer in a small village in South of Holland.
Speaker 2: Do you remember moments when you were hearing fighting on the streets, fire?

Speaker 1: No, the only the only thing I remember very well, if we talk about war action, that was the fight around the Battle of Arnhem. The Battle of Arnhem was one of the greatest battles in in the Second World War because they believed that if they could take the bridge of Arnhem, they could invade Germany, and it would be the end of the war.
Speaker 2: You saw the parachutes?
Speaker 1: Yeah, they came in the where I lived, they came all around me.
Speaker 2: You remember?

Speaker 1: Yes, I remember personally very well, and also I remember very well how the American parachutists came down, the Germans shot at them, and there were many of these parachutists were killed, and they were not able to get the bridge, and they lost.
The reason that I come here, and the reason that I tell the story,
Speaker 2: Yeah.
Speaker 1: is that we want the people, the world also, to remember, and not to forget, and not to forgive.
And it's my task, as long as I live, to tell the people what happened, so it won't happen again.
